title: Partition and Rebuild
focus: One-pass partitioning, augmented containers, and reconstructing a tree from its shadows.

cards.title: Dutch National Flag
patterns: Do not advance on a swap from the back
cards.trigger: Partition an array into two or three buckets in one pass with O(1) space.
cards.recall: Write sort-colors from memory. Then answer the single line everyone gets wrong: after swapping with `high`, why do you NOT increment `mid`?
useWhen: Sort an array of three distinct values
Move all zeros, or all of one property, to one end
Quicksort partition step, and Quickselect
Partition around a pivot for kth largest
Segregate by any binary or ternary predicate in place
template: #  (high, n)  = 2s     everything in [mid, high] is unclassified
high -= 1              # NOT mid += 1: the swapped-in value is unseen
keyInsights: State the three region invariants before writing the loop. The pointer updates then follow mechanically
The value swapped in from `high` has never been examined, so `mid` must stay put. The value swapped in from `low` is already known to be a 1
`mid <= high`, not `<`, or you leave the last element unclassified
cards.trap: 'Do it with counting sort instead.' Two passes and O(1) space too, but it fails the moment the elements carry payload rather than being bare labels.

cards.title: Augmented Stack
cards.trigger: You need a stack that also answers a running query, minimum, maximum or sum, in O(1).
cards.recall: Write Min Stack from memory using the pair approach. Then answer: why does storing `min so far` per entry work, when a separate min variable does not survive a pop?
useWhen: Min stack, max stack, stack with running sum
Max frequency stack
Any structure that must answer an aggregate in O(1) under push and pop
Queue with a maximum, built from two augmented stacks
Undo systems that must report a summary of the current state
template: cur_min = x if not self.st else min(x, self.st[-1][1])
# Space-tighter variant: a second stack that only grows on a new minimum
if not self.mins or x <= self.mins[-1]:   # <= matters for duplicates
keyInsights: Each entry remembers the answer for the stack as it was, so popping restores the previous answer for free
In the two-stack variant, `<=` not `<`. With `<`, duplicate minima get popped once and lost
The same idea extends to any aggregate that is cheap to combine but not cheap to recompute
cards.trap: 'Constant extra space, not O(n).' There is an encoding trick storing 2*x - min, and its real cost is overflow risk. Mention the trick and its cost, do not pretend it is free.

cards.title: Rebuild from Traversals
cards.trigger: You are handed two traversals and asked for the tree.
cards.recall: Write the preorder-plus-inorder construction from memory. Then answer: which pairs of traversals uniquely determine a binary tree, and which famous pair does not?
useWhen: Construct from preorder and inorder, or from inorder and postorder
Construct a BST from preorder alone, sorted order is implied
Convert a sorted array or sorted list into a balanced BST
Verify preorder serialisation without building anything
Any 'reconstruct the structure' phrasing
template: pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}   # O(1) split lookup
def go(lo, hi):                    # inorder range [lo, hi]
node.left  = go(lo, mid - 1)   # left MUST be built first:
node.right = go(mid + 1, hi)   # preorder consumes left subtree next
# Postorder + inorder: walk postorder BACKWARDS and build right before left

problem.name: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

keyInsights: Left before right is not stylistic. Preorder lays out the entire left subtree immediately after the root
Without the index map, finding the split is a linear scan and the whole thing degrades to O(n^2)
Preorder plus postorder does NOT determine a binary tree uniquely. It does for a full binary tree. That is the follow-up
cards.trap: 'The values are not unique.' The index map collapses and the split becomes ambiguous. You must say so rather than produce a plausible wrong tree.

cards.title: Palindrome Expansion
cards.trigger: Counting or measuring palindromic substrings, where the check itself is the expensive part.
cards.recall: Write the expand-around-centre counter from memory. Then answer: why are there 2n-1 centres and not n, and what is the space advantage over the DP table?
useWhen: Longest palindromic substring
Count all palindromic substrings
Palindrome partitioning, precompute an is-palindrome table first
Shortest palindrome by prefix
Longest palindromic subsequence, which is a different, interval DP
template: # Expand around centre: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Prefer this.
for c in range(2 * n - 1):          # 2n-1 centres: n odd, n-1 even
while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
# Table form, when a later DP needs is_pal[i][j] anyway
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):          # i descending: needs i+1 ready
if s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or is_pal[i + 1][j - 1]):
keyInsights: n odd centres on characters plus n-1 even centres between them. The `c // 2, c // 2 + c % 2` line encodes both
The table version must fill i descending, because is_pal[i][j] depends on is_pal[i+1][j-1]
Expand-around-centre is O(1) space and easier to write correctly. Reach for the table only when a later stage needs it
cards.trap: 'Do it in O(n).' That is Manacher's. You are not expected to write it, but you should name it and say it is linear, then offer the O(n^2) you can actually get right.

cards.title: Minimum Spanning Tree
cards.trigger: Connect every node at minimum total edge weight, with no cycles.
cards.recall: Write Kruskal from memory using the DSU you already know. Then answer: on a complete graph with a thousand points, which of Prim or Kruskal do you choose, and why?
useWhen: Minimum cost to connect all points or all cities
Cluster by cutting the k-1 largest MST edges
Network design with a redundancy budget
Critical connections where you need the cheapest backbone
Any 'connect everything as cheaply as possible' phrasing
template: # Kruskal: sort every edge, take it if it joins two components
def kruskal(n, edges):                  # edges are (w, u, v)
for w, u, v in edges:
if dsu.union(u, v):             # False means it would form a cycle
# Prim: grow one tree, always take the cheapest edge leaving it

complexity.time: O(E log E) Kruskal, O(E log V) Prim

problem.name: Min Cost to Connect All Points

keyInsights: Kruskal is your DSU plus a sort. If DSU is solid, Kruskal is ten lines and nothing new
On a complete graph E is V^2, so Kruskal sorts a million edges. Prim with an implicit adjacency wins there
Both are greedy and both are provably optimal via the cut property. Naming the cut property is a strong signal
cards.trap: 'Is the MST unique?' Yes if all edge weights are distinct. With ties there can be several, all of the same total. Know that answer cold.
